--- title: "Scaling single-cell phenotyping with Cellpose and cloud GPU compute" date: 'January 1, 2025' abstract-title: "Summary" --- ## Abstract A reusable, cloud-scalable pipeline that pairs Cellpose-SAM segmentation with on-demand GPU compute (Modal + S3) for single-cell phenotyping of high-content microscopy, demonstrated on a two-species yeast panel (*S. cerevisiae* vs. *S. pombe*). ---- :::{.callout-note title="AI usage disclosure" collapse="true"} This is a placeholder for the AI usage disclosure. Once all authors sign the AI code form on Airtable, SlackBot will message you an AI disclosure that you should place here. ::: ## Purpose High-content microscopy can generate more images than a single workstation can segment in a reasonable amount of time. The main challenge is often the supporting workflow: transferring images, provisioning GPUs, running segmentation consistently, and collecting standardized per-cell measurements. This pub presents a pipeline that combines Cellpose-SAM with on-demand GPU compute to process large microscopy datasets without requiring users to build and maintain that infrastructure. This notebook pub demonstrates two points: 1. Cellpose-SAM plus cloud GPU compute is a reliable way to scale single-cell phenotyping across large microscopy datasets. 2. The phenotyping outputs derived from the segmentation have the capacity to resolve gross morphological differences between strains or conditions. This work is intended for researchers developing high-throughput microscopy workflows or deciding how to scale segmentation and phenotyping. You can run it on the example data or adapt the same workflow—file I/O, segmentation, parallel execution, and per-cell measurement—to your own images. The biological example serves as a validation dataset rather than a source of new biological conclusions. For background on the underlying tools, see the Cellpose-SAM literature [@pachitariu2025cellpose] and the [Modal documentation](https://modal.com/docs). ## How the pipeline fits together :::{.callout-note title="Draft figure" collapse="false"} A designed hero figure (in progress with Audrey) will replace the schematic below. The Mermaid diagram is a functional stand-in that captures the intended flow. ::: The workflow is a straight line from raw images to per-cell measurements, with one key property: the segmentation step is identical whether it runs on one machine or hundreds of GPU containers. Scale is a deployment choice, not a code rewrite. ```{mermaid} flowchart LR A["Brightfield ND2s
datasets/<id>/raw/"] --> B["File I/O + preprocessing
arcadia-microscopy-tools"] B --> C["Segmentation
Cellpose-SAM → label masks"] C --> D{"Scale-out
one worker per image"} D --> E["Derived artifacts
masks · overlays · measurements"] E --> F["Analysis
pooled per-cell morphology"] P["Plate map
well → strain"] --> F ``` 1. **Input:** brightfield ND2s in object storage, organized as `datasets//raw/`, with a plate map linking wells to strains. 2. **File I/O and preprocessing:** `arcadia-microscopy-tools` handles ND2 reading, channel and pixel-size metadata, and percentile rescaling. 3. **Segmentation:** Cellpose-SAM produces label masks; border-touching cells are dropped. 4. **Scale-out:** one worker per image is fanned across on-demand GPU containers, each reading from and writing to shared cloud storage. 5. **Outputs (`derived/`):** label-mask TIFFs, outline-overlay JPGs for QC, and per-cell measurement CSVs (regionprops, in microns where the pixel size is known). 6. **Analysis:** pooled per-cell measurements joined to the plate map for morphology comparisons across strains. ## A two-species yeast panel The validation dataset contains brightfield images of two diploid yeast species selected for their visually distinct morphologies: ovoid budding yeast and rod-shaped fission yeast. | Species | Strain | Wells | | --- | --- | --- | | *S. cerevisiae* | `BY4743` | K01–K04, L01–L04 | | *S. pombe* | `SP286` | K05–K08, L05–L08 | : Plate map for the two-species panel {#tbl-plate-map} Each of the 16 wells was imaged at four fields arranged in a 2 × 2 grid, yielding 64 ND2 files. Images were acquired with NIS-Elements JOBS. Within each species, the wells are technical replicates. The `plate-map.csv` file maps each well to its genus, species, strain, and ploidy. NIS-Elements filenames encode the well and field; for example, `WellK01_PointK01_0000_Channelbrightfield_Seq0000.nd2` identifies the first field in well K01. Joining the well identifier to the plate map attaches the corresponding sample metadata to each image and, after segmentation, to each cell. Each ND2 file also stores acquisition metadata, including the objective, pixel size, exposure time, etc. Because these settings are consistent across the dataset, the next code cell reads one representative file from either S3 or the public Zenodo archive and parses its metadata with `arcadia-microscopy-tools`. The pipeline uses the pixel-size metadata to convert spatial measurements from pixels to physical units. The dataset is available from the Zenodo archive (record `XXXXXXXX`; DOI: `10.5281/zenodo.XXXXXXXX`). Local execution reads the record identifier from `ZENODO_RECORD_ID` or `CSCP_ZENODO_RECORD_ID`. Arcadia users with AWS access can read the same files directly from S3. ::: {#9cabe75c .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="true" code-summary="Code to load the example ND2 and extract metadata"} import subprocess from pathlib import Path import pandas as pd from arcadia_microscopy_tools.nikon import parse_nd2 DATASET_ID = "20260611_141152_330" EXAMPLE_ND2 = "WellK01_PointK01_0000_Channelbrightfield_Seq0000.nd2" RAW_DIR = Path("scratch/sample_data") / DATASET_ID / "raw" nd2_path = RAW_DIR / EXAMPLE_ND2 if not nd2_path.exists(): RAW_DIR.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True) src = f"s3://cloud-scaled-cell-phenotyping/datasets/{DATASET_ID}/raw/{EXAMPLE_ND2}" try: subprocess.run(["aws", "s3", "cp", src, str(nd2_path)], check=True, capture_output=True) except (FileNotFoundError, subprocess.CalledProcessError): from analysis.sample_data import fetch_sample_nd2s nd2_path = fetch_sample_nd2s(DATASET_ID, RAW_DIR, limit=1)[0] meta = parse_nd2(nd2_path) cm = meta.channel_metadata_list[0] pd.DataFrame.from_dict( { "file": nd2_path.name, "channel": cm.channel.name, "objective": cm.optics.objective, "magnification": cm.optics.magnification, "NA": cm.optics.numerical_aperture, "pixel_size_um": cm.resolution.xy_step_um, "exposure_s": cm.acquisition.exposure_time_s, }, orient="index", columns=["value"], ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ```{=html}

``` ::: ::: ## Demo: single-cell segmentation at scale The code cells below run the full pipeline from start to finish. Cellpose-SAM [@pachitariu2025cellpose], implemented through `arcadia-microscopy-tools`, segments cells in the brightfield ND2 files and generates label masks, quality-control overlays, and per-cell measurement tables. The segmentation code runs in one of two interchangeable modes, chosen automatically so the notebook runs with or without connecting to our cloud infrastructure. All downstream cells run unchanged in either mode. ::: {.panel-tabset} ## Scaled execution (Modal + S3) For Arcadia users with access to our cloud infrastructure, each ND2 file is processed by a separate GPU worker [@modal]. The worker reads the file from S3 and writes the resulting artifacts back to the bucket. This mode processes full plates efficiently by running files in parallel on GPUs. ## Local execution (no cloud account required) For external users, the same Cellpose-SAM code runs locally, using the CPU by default. Example ND2 files download from the public Zenodo archive once the record id is set (`CSCP_ZENODO_RECORD_ID` or `ZENODO_RECORD_ID`); until then the local path fails loudly instead of guessing. The `limit` parameter keeps the run short. This mode can also process full plates, but sequential CPU execution is slower. ::: The next code cell triggers the run. In either mode, `run_demo` processes $n=$`limit` images and returns the same result object, so the downstream cells remain unchanged. A progress bar advances as each image finishes and reports its cell count. Because the sorted file list begins with well K01, the three-image local sample contains only *S. cerevisiae*. Full-plate measurements and quality-control overlays are loaded separately below. ::: {.callout-note title="Forcing a backend" collapse="true"} Set `CSCP_FORCE_LOCAL=1` to force the local path, or pass `backend="modal"` / `backend="local"` to `run_demo`. Details live in the [setup guide](pages/SETUP.qmd). ::: ::: {#b282a465 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="true" code-summary="Code to trigger cell segmentation"} import time from analysis.runner import run_demo # Three images in both backends. Local CPU cannot do a full plate in a demo; # files sort from well K01, so this sample is S. cerevisiae only. # Full-plate measurements and QC overlays load separately below. LIMIT = 3 CELL_DIAMETER = 30 # pixels CELLPROP_THRESHOLD = 3.0 started = time.time() run = run_demo( DATASET_ID, limit=LIMIT, diameter=CELL_DIAMETER, cellprob_threshold=CELLPROP_THRESHOLD, ) elapsed = time.time() - started if run.backend == "modal": print(f"[modal] Wrote artifacts to s3://cloud-scaled-cell-phenotyping/{run.output_prefix}/") else: print(f"[local] Wrote artifacts to {run.output_prefix}") print(f"Segmented {len(run.results)} image(s), {len(run.failures)} failure(s) in {elapsed:.1f}s.") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` Segmenting: 0%| | 0/3 [00:00/measurements/` in shared storage, so you don't have to re-segment to analyze them. `MEASUREMENTS_SOURCE = "auto"` loads the full precomputed table for every well from S3 or Zenodo, so the analysis includes both species even when the demo only segmented a few images. The Zenodo path uses the same record-id placeholder as the sample ND2s: unset until the archive is published, then `CSCP_ZENODO_RECORD_ID` or `ZENODO_RECORD_ID`. ::: {#d0ee1968 .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} # "auto" loads the full plate from S3 or Zenodo; "run" uses only the demo images. MEASUREMENTS_SOURCE = "auto" # "run" | "auto" | "modal" | "zenodo" ``` ::: ::: {#dd328ce2 .cell execution_count=5} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 113454 cells across 2 species. ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=5} ```{=html}

``` ::: ::: ## Shape alone separates the two species The per-cell measurements are the pipeline's actual product, so the fair test of the pipeline is whether they support the kind of analysis you'd want to do next. We ask the simplest version of that question: given nothing but per-cell shape, can you tell the two yeasts apart? *S. cerevisiae* is an ovoid budding yeast and *S. pombe* is a rod, so the expected answer is yes — and that's the point. A pipeline that failed this test wouldn't be worth scaling. We're testing the measurements, not discovering biology. Two steps follow. First we look at the joint distribution of the two features that should carry most of the signal, cell area and eccentricity. Then we rank every shape feature by how well it separates the species on its own. Before any of that, we gate on cell area. Segmentation returns some objects that aren't single cells: fragments and debris at the small end, and clumps that Cellpose resolved as a single mask at the large end (the largest object in the full-plate table is about 1,270 µm², roughly fifty times the median *S. cerevisiae* cell). We keep objects between 5 and 100 µm², an area-equivalent circular diameter of 2.5–11.3 µm, which brackets a plausible single yeast cell. The gate is deliberately loose: it drops about 1% of objects and isn't tuned to flatter the analysis. ::: {#7a56e334 .cell execution_count=6} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="true" code-summary="Code to set up the analysis and gate on cell area"} import arcadia_pycolor as apc import numpy as np import plotly.graph_objects as go from plotly.subplots import make_subplots apc.plotly.setup() GROUP_COL = "species" REFERENCE = "cerevisiae" # the species the others are compared against POSITIVE = "pombe" # the "positive" class for AUC AREA_COL = "area_um2" if "area_um2" in labeled.columns else "area" AREA_LABEL = "cell area (µm²)" if AREA_COL == "area_um2" else "cell area (px)" # Plausible-single-cell gate. 5-100 µm² is an area-equivalent circular diameter of # 2.5-11.3 µm: below it, debris and partial masks; above it, merged clumps. MIN_AREA_UM2 = 5.0 MAX_AREA_UM2 = 100.0 measured = labeled.dropna(subset=[GROUP_COL, AREA_COL]) # The gate is written in µm², so it only applies when the pixel size was known. in_gate = ( measured[AREA_COL].between(MIN_AREA_UM2, MAX_AREA_UM2) if AREA_COL == "area_um2" else pd.Series(True, index=measured.index) ) analysis_df = measured.loc[in_gate].copy() present = list(analysis_df[GROUP_COL].unique()) groups = ([REFERENCE] if REFERENCE in present else []) + sorted( g for g in present if g != REFERENCE ) # Italicized "S. pombe"-style labels and a stable color per species, from the plate map. genus_by_species = plate_map.drop_duplicates(GROUP_COL).set_index(GROUP_COL)["genus"] DISPLAY = {species: f"{genus_by_species[species][0]}. {species}" for species in groups} COLORS = dict( zip(groups, [apc.aegean.hex_code, apc.amber.hex_code, apc.seaweed.hex_code], strict=False) ) n_dropped = int((~in_gate).sum()) print( f"{len(analysis_df):,} of {len(measured):,} cells pass the " f"{MIN_AREA_UM2:g}-{MAX_AREA_UM2:g} µm² gate " f"({n_dropped:,} dropped, {n_dropped / len(measured):.2%})." ) print( f"{len(groups)} species across {analysis_df['well'].nunique()} well(s) and " f"{analysis_df['image'].nunique()} image(s): {', '.join(groups)}" ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 111,929 of 113,454 cells pass the 5-100 µm² gate (1,525 dropped, 1.34%). 2 species across 16 well(s) and 64 image(s): cerevisiae, pombe ``` ::: ::: ::: {#fcc4b8f6 .cell execution_count=7} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="true" code-summary="Code for the area-vs-eccentricity figure"} # Every cell is used for the marginal boxes; the scatter shows a random subsample per # species, since 112,000 overplotted markers read as two solid blobs (and bloat the page). POINTS_PER_SPECIES = 5000 rng = np.random.default_rng(0) def box_stats(values): """Quartiles and Tukey fences for a Plotly box trace built from precomputed statistics.""" q1, median, q3 = np.percentile(values, [25, 50, 75]) iqr = q3 - q1 return dict( q1=[q1], median=[median], q3=[q3], lowerfence=[max(values.min(), q1 - 1.5 * iqr)], upperfence=[min(values.max(), q3 + 1.5 * iqr)], mean=[values.mean()], ) fig = make_subplots( rows=2, cols=2, column_widths=[0.85, 0.15], row_heights=[0.15, 0.85], shared_xaxes=True, shared_yaxes=True, horizontal_spacing=0.02, vertical_spacing=0.02, ) for species in groups: cells = analysis_df[analysis_df[GROUP_COL] == species] color = COLORS[species] shown = cells.iloc[ rng.choice(len(cells), size=min(POINTS_PER_SPECIES, len(cells)), replace=False) ] fig.add_trace( go.Scattergl( x=shown[AREA_COL], y=shown["eccentricity"], mode="markers", showlegend=False, marker=dict(color=color, size=3, opacity=0.4, line=dict(width=0)), hovertemplate=f"{species}
area %{{x:.1f}} µm²
ecc. %{{y:.2f}}", ), row=2, col=1, ) # A legend-only proxy, so the key shows a full-size, full-opacity marker. fig.add_trace( go.Scatter( x=[None], y=[None], mode="markers", name=f"{DISPLAY[species]} (n = {len(cells):,})", marker=dict(color=color, size=9), ), row=2, col=1, ) box_kwargs = dict( showlegend=False, fillcolor=color, line=dict(color=apc.charcoal.hex_code, width=1), width=0.45, hoverinfo="skip", ) fig.add_trace( go.Box(**box_stats(cells[AREA_COL].to_numpy()), y=[species], orientation="h", **box_kwargs), row=1, col=1, ) fig.add_trace( go.Box(**box_stats(cells["eccentricity"].to_numpy()), x=[species], **box_kwargs), row=2, col=2, ) fig.update_xaxes(title_text=AREA_LABEL, range=[0, MAX_AREA_UM2], row=2, col=1) fig.update_yaxes(title_text="eccentricity", range=[0, 1.02], row=2, col=1) for row, col in ((1, 1), (2, 2)): # the marginals borrow their scale from the scatter fig.update_xaxes(showticklabels=False, ticks="", showline=False, row=row, col=col) fig.update_yaxes(showticklabels=False, ticks="", showline=False, row=row, col=col) fig.update_layout( width=720, height=560, title="Area and eccentricity split the panel into two populations", legend=dict( x=0.99, y=0.03, xanchor="right", yanchor="bottom", bgcolor="rgba(255,255,255,0.75)" ), ) apc.plotly.style_plot(fig, monospaced_axes="xy", row=2, col=1) fig.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: The two clouds barely touch. *S. pombe* traces a tight arc, which is what fission yeast morphology predicts: it grows by extending its tips at roughly constant width, so a cell gets larger and more elongated at the same time, and area and eccentricity rise together over the cell cycle. *S. cerevisiae* instead fills a broad, rounder cloud with a tail toward small area and low eccentricity — mostly small buds. The marginal boxes show where the separation actually comes from: the area distributions overlap substantially, since a large budding yeast is the size of a small fission yeast, while the eccentricity distributions hardly overlap at all. ### Ranking every shape feature Area and eccentricity are two of the nine shape features the pipeline reports. To rank all of them, we use the area under the ROC curve for each feature on its own — the probability that a randomly chosen *S. pombe* cell scores higher than a randomly chosen *S. cerevisiae* cell. An AUC of 0.5 means the feature is useless and 1.0 means the two distributions don't overlap at all. It's a rank statistic, so the long tails in these distributions don't distort it. We also report a Mann–Whitney p-value on the well-level medians, not on the individual cells. Cells from the same well share a field of view, a focus plane, and an illumination profile, so a test across all 100,000+ cells would treat those shared conditions as independent observations and return p ≈ 0 for every feature. The table instead compares sixteen well medians, eight per species. With eight versus eight, the smallest two-sided p-value is 1.6 × 10⁻⁴, and several features reach it because their well medians do not overlap. Those wells are technical replicates, so the test measures consistency across wells rather than a difference between the species. ::: {#c472595a .cell execution_count=8} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="true" code-summary="Code to rank shape features by how well each one separates the species"} from scipy.stats import mannwhitneyu from sklearn.metrics import roc_auc_score # Shape only. Orientation is an arbitrary lab-frame angle, the centroids are positions, and # the brightfield intensities describe illumination as much as they describe the cell. FEATURES = { "area_um2": "area (µm²)", "area_convex_um2": "convex area (µm²)", "perimeter_um": "perimeter (µm)", "axis_major_length_um": "major axis (µm)", "axis_minor_length_um": "minor axis (µm)", "eccentricity": "eccentricity", "solidity": "solidity", "circularity": "circularity", "volume_um3": "volume (µm³)", } FEATURES = {col: label for col, label in FEATURES.items() if col in analysis_df.columns} is_positive = (analysis_df[GROUP_COL] == POSITIVE).to_numpy() well_medians = analysis_df.groupby(["well", GROUP_COL])[list(FEATURES)].median().reset_index() rows = [] for col, label in FEATURES.items(): auc = roc_auc_score(is_positive, analysis_df[col]) _, p_well = mannwhitneyu( well_medians.loc[well_medians[GROUP_COL] == POSITIVE, col], well_medians.loc[well_medians[GROUP_COL] == REFERENCE, col], alternative="two-sided", ) rows.append( { "feature": label, f"median, {REFERENCE}": round(analysis_df.loc[~is_positive, col].median(), 2), f"median, {POSITIVE}": round(analysis_df.loc[is_positive, col].median(), 2), # Flip AUCs below 0.5 so every feature is scored in its discriminating direction. "AUC": round(max(auc, 1 - auc), 3), "well-level p": f"{p_well:.1e}", } ) feature_stats = pd.DataFrame(rows).sort_values("AUC", ascending=False).reset_index(drop=True) feature_stats ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=8} ```{=html}

``` ::: ::: Eccentricity leads at an AUC of 0.995, with circularity and major-axis length close behind: all three are measuring elongation. The size features land lower (area at 0.951), and the two features that describe neither elongation nor size, solidity and minor-axis length, are barely better than a coin flip. That last result is the one worth noting: fission yeast and budding yeast are about the same width, so a feature that only knew cell width would have almost nothing to work with. ## What this demo does not show - **Scope:** gross morphology only, from single-channel brightfield images. Staining- or fluorescence-based phenotyping is a natural extension, not shown here. - **Compute and cost:** the scaled path relies on paid GPU compute and cloud storage. The local CPU fallback is scoped to a few images so anyone can reproduce the core result without an account, but it does not exercise the scale-out. - **Replication:** a single dataset with multiple wells per species (technical, not biological, replicates). Enough to show the pipeline produces stable, species-resolved phenotypes; not enough to make claims about the organisms. ## Acknowledgements Overview-figure design by Audrey. Contributors and author list to be added. The pipeline combines [`arcadia-microscopy-tools`](https://github.com/Arcadia-Science/arcadia-microscopy-tools) for file I/O, preprocessing, and measurements [@amt]; Cellpose-SAM for segmentation [@pachitariu2025cellpose]; and [Modal](https://modal.com/) for on-demand GPU compute [@modal], with artifacts stored on Amazon S3. ::: {.callout-note title="Run it yourself"} Environment setup and both backends (Modal + S3, or local CPU on the Zenodo sample) live in the [setup guide](pages/SETUP.qmd). ::: ## Appendix {#sec-appendix} `SegmentConfig` knobs forwarded to Cellpose-SAM, plus the Modal scale-out parameters. Defaults match a typical brightfield yeast field; change them in `run_demo(...)` if your cells differ. | Parameter | Default | Role | | --- | --- | --- | | `diameter` | `None` (30 px) | Expected cell diameter in pixels | | `flow_threshold` | `0.4` | Mask quality filter (higher is stricter) | | `cellprob_threshold` | `0.0` | Cell-probability cutoff (higher yields fewer, more confident masks) | | `percentile_low` / `percentile_high` | `1.0` / `99.0` | Contrast-stretch window before segmentation | | `gpu` | `L4` | Modal GPU type | | `max_containers` | `10` | Ceiling on concurrent GPU workers | : Segmentation and scale-out parameters {#tbl-segment-config}
